mythology.lead: Ōsaka began as the ancient port of Naniwa, gateway to the Asian continent and briefly an imperial capital. It later became the merchant city par excellence — the 'kitchen of the nation' — and the fortress from which Toyotomi Hideyoshi sought to rule a unified Japan.

myths.title: Naniwa, the First Imperial Port
myths.text: Long before it was called Ōsaka, the area was known as Naniwa. The Nihon Shoki records that Emperor Nintoku's great tomb rose on the Osaka plain, and in 645 Emperor Kōtoku moved the capital to Naniwa Nagara Toyosaki-no-miya, making it Japan's first official capital. The city of Ōsaka notes that Naniwazu port served as the arrival point for envoys, Buddhism, ceramics, and metallurgy from Korea and China, technologies that then spread across the archipelago.

myths.title: Shitennō-ji and Prince Shōtoku
myths.text: In 593 Prince Shōtoku founded Shitennō-ji, one of Japan's oldest Buddhist temples, in what is now Ōsaka. The temple was both a religious centre and a diplomatic statement: it marked the region's role as a point of contact with the continental mainland. Shitennō-ji's pagoda and gate still stand, a reminder that Ōsaka's identity was shaped by international exchange as much as by trade.

myths.title: Hideyoshi's Castle Town
myths.text: In 1583 Toyotomi Hideyoshi, who had completed the military unification of Japan, began construction of Ōsaka Castle on the site of the former Ishiyama Hongan-ji fortress. He intended the castle to be the centre of a new political order. After his death the Toyotomi were destroyed by Tokugawa Ieyasu in the sieges of 1614–1615, but the castle kept its symbolic place as the heart of the Kansai merchant capital.

myths.title: The Nation's Kitchen
myths.text: During the Edo period (1603–1868) Ōsaka became Japan's principal distribution centre for rice, sake, and luxury goods. The city's network of canals earned it the nickname tenka no daidokoro, 'the nation's kitchen'. Merchant culture flourished here: bunraku puppet theatre, kabuki, and the money markets of Dōjima made Ōsaka an urban culture distinct from the aristocracy of Kyōto and the samurai of Edo.
